public_rationale: The disclosures make lower training cost plausible, including a later $294,000 estimate for the R1 post-training project. But that figure excludes base training, and the V3 figure measures a different model's training. Neither establishes the complete comparison Marcus asserted. His accounting basis and comparator are also unspecified.
limitations: Unresolved does not mean the cheaper-training claim is false.
Rental-equivalent compute estimates are not audited total expenditure.
The later R1 disclosure was considered; it was not excluded merely because it appeared after the post.

statement.excerpt: DeepSeek r1 is not smarter than earlier models, just trained more cheaply
statement.document_title: Five things most people don't seem to understand about DeepSeek

our_interpretation: The ordinary reading is lower training cost for a complete, comparably capable model, including its base-model training and subsequent reasoning training.
This does not require counting all corporate investment as training cost. Any inclusion of experiments, personnel or data expenses must be consistent across models.
The observation concerns the training that produced the original January 20 release. Its starting date is unspecified.
Marcus cites no cost source or accounting basis in the supplied text, so accounting_basis is unknown.
criteria.support_condition: Comparable cost records establish that producing the complete R1 model cost less than producing comparably capable preceding frontier models.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Comparable cost records establish that producing R1 cost as much as or more than the relevant preceding models.
